title: difflense - A Privacy-First, Browser-Based Git Diff Viewer
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: difflense is an open-source, client-side diff viewer that transforms raw git diff output into readable, shareable views without ever uploading your code to a server.
contents:
Sharing code changes with teammates should be simple. You generate a diff, send it over, and they review it. In practice, the available tools introduce friction at every step: some require uploading diffs or entire repositories to a third-party server, others produce clunky displays that make reviews harder than reading raw terminal output, and many generate share links that break for large diffs. I kept hitting the same problem: I wanted to paste or upload a diff, view it cleanly in the browser, and share a link, all without my code leaving my machine.

So I built difflense, a lightweight, open-source, browser-first diff viewer that parses and renders diffs entirely on the client side and generates shareable URLs without any server involvement.

What difflense Does

At its core, difflense is a client-side application that takes Git or unified diff text as input and renders it with syntax highlighting and line numbers. The key capabilities include:

  • Unified and side-by-side views. Toggle between an inline view that shows changes sequentially and a split-pane view that places old and new code next to each other for direct comparison.
  • Shareable links. Generate URLs that embed the diff data directly in the link itself. When someone opens the link, the browser decodes and renders the diff. No server stores or transmits the data.
  • Complete privacy. No backend, no telemetry, no data storage. Everything is processed in the browser. Your code never leaves your machine unless you choose to share the generated link.
  • Zero setup. Works with any diff text you already have from git diff, git show, or any diff -u output. No installation, no account, no configuration.

The Privacy Problem With Existing Tools

Most diff-sharing tools follow the same pattern: upload your diff to a server, the server stores it, and the server generates a link. This model has several problems for professional development work. Proprietary code should not be uploaded to third-party servers without explicit approval. Even with "private" links, the data exists on infrastructure you do not control. Compliance requirements in some organizations explicitly prohibit sending source code to external services.

difflense sidesteps all of these concerns by never transmitting the diff anywhere. The rendering happens in your browser. The shareable link embeds a compressed version of the diff in the URL itself, so the recipient's browser does the decoding and rendering too. No server is involved at any point.

How the Shareable Links Work

Embedding raw diff text directly in a URL runs into a practical problem: URLs have length limits enforced by browsers and servers (typically around 2,000 to 8,000 characters depending on the stack). A diff for even a modest change can easily exceed this. difflense handles this with a two-step process executed entirely in the browser:

  1. Compression. The raw diff text is compressed using Brotli, a highly efficient compression algorithm. For typical diff text with its repetitive structure (file headers, line prefixes, whitespace patterns), Brotli achieves substantial size reduction.
  2. Encoding. The compressed bytes are Base64-encoded with URL-safe character substitutions, producing a string that can be safely embedded in a URL fragment or query parameter.

When someone opens the generated link, the process reverses: the browser decodes the Base64 string, decompresses the Brotli data, and difflense renders the resulting diff. The entire round trip happens on the client side.

Early versions used only Base64 encoding without compression, but long diffs produced URLs that exceeded browser limits or broke when pasted into messaging apps. Adding Brotli compression before encoding reduced the URL length dramatically and made large diffs practically shareable.

Practical Use Cases

Quick Code Reviews Without Repo Access

You need a contractor or a colleague from another team to review a specific change, but they do not have access to your repository. Generate a diff, paste it into difflense, create a shareable link, and send it. They get a clean, syntax-highlighted view without needing to clone anything.

Documentation and Design Reviews

When discussing architectural changes, a readable diff is often more useful than a written description. Embed a difflense link in your design document or issue tracker to give reviewers the exact code context alongside the discussion.

Bug Reports and Issue Tracking

Attach a difflense link to a bug report to show exactly what changed between the working and broken states. The link serves as a permanent, self-contained snapshot of the change.

Teaching and Demonstrations

Show students or junior developers how a specific change looks without requiring them to set up the project, clone the repository, or navigate a complex PR interface. The link opens directly to a clean diff view.

Step-by-Step: Generating and Sharing a Diff

1. Create a Diff From Git

Use any standard Git diff command to produce the text input:

# Unstaged working tree changes
git diff > my-changes.diff

# Staged changes
git diff --staged > staged-changes.diff

# Compare two commits
git diff abc1234 def5678 > commits.diff

# Compare two branches
git diff main..feature/my-feature > branch-diff.diff

# Single file between commits
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD -- src/app/service.js > service.diff

2. Open difflense

Navigate to the hosted instance or your own deployment:

https://difflense.nbslabs.dev

3. Paste or Upload

Paste the contents of your .diff file into the input area, or use the file upload control to select the file directly.

4. Choose a View Mode

Toggle between unified (inline) and side-by-side views depending on your preference or the complexity of the change.

5. Review and Share

Inspect the rendered diff with syntax highlighting and line numbers. Click the share button to generate a compressed, encoded URL. Copy the link and send it to your team. Anyone who opens it will see the identical rendered view in their browser, with all processing happening locally.

Best Practices

  • Strip sensitive data before sharing. difflense does not upload your code, but any data embedded in the shareable link is visible to anyone who has that link. Remove API keys, credentials, or other secrets from diffs before generating share links.
  • Add context when sharing links. A diff link alone can be confusing without a short note explaining the PR context, the problem being solved, or what to focus on during review.
  • Use for focused changes. difflense works best for sharing specific, focused diffs rather than entire repository comparisons. For full-repository code review, a Git hosting platform's PR interface is still the better tool.

Contributing

difflense is open source and welcomes contributions. The repository is available at github.com/nbslabs/difflense. Whether it is reporting bugs, suggesting features, or submitting pull requests for improvements like additional diff format support, theme options, or performance optimizations, contributions help the project grow.

Key Takeaways

  1. Privacy by architecture, not policy. difflense does not rely on promises about data handling. The architecture itself prevents data from leaving your browser.
  2. Client-side compression makes sharing practical. Brotli compression combined with Base64 encoding allows even large diffs to be embedded in shareable URLs without exceeding browser limits.
  3. Zero friction for reviewers. Recipients do not need accounts, repository access, or any setup. They click a link and see the diff.
  4. Right tool for the right job. difflense fills a specific gap: quick, private, shareable diff viewing. It complements, rather than replaces, full-featured code review platforms.

If you need a quick, private, and zero-setup way to turn git diff output into a readable, shareable view, difflense is a practical tool. It is particularly suited for teams that value privacy, work with sensitive codebases, or simply want to share changes without the overhead of granting repository access.
